title: VELTHEPU SRINIVAS AND OTHERS versus STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH (NOW STATE OF TELANGANA) AND ANR.
respondent: STATE OF ANDHRA PRADESH (NOW STATE OF TELANGANA) AND ANR.
case_title: Velthepu Srinivas and Others v. State of Andhra Pradesh (Now State of Telangana) and Anr.
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302, s.34; IPC s.304 Part II
aggravating_circumstances: Political animosity, use of weapons, multiple assaults
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302/34 IPC, life imprisonment
high_court_outcome: Confirmed conviction and sentence for A-1, A-2, A-4; modified for A-3
offence_finally_established: Murder under s.302 IPC for A-1, A-2, A-4; culpable homicide not amounting to murder under s.304 Part II IPC for A-3
neutral_facts: The accused, who were part of the same family, were involved in a political dispute with the victim, who was from the same village. On 15.11.2001, the victim was traveling in an auto-rickshaw when the accused stopped the vehicle and dragged the victim to the house of one of the accused. The accused then assaulted the victim with various weapons, including an axe, sword, stone, and knife, leading to the victim's death. The prosecution presented eyewitness accounts, a post-mortem report, and recovered weapons as evidence.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment / Death
physical_harm: Severe bleeding injuries leading to death
number_of_offences: Four accused charged, three finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimonies of eyewitnesses, including PW-6, who was in the auto-rickshaw with the deceased, and the post-mortem report indicating the cause of death as cardio-pulmonary arrest due to spinal cord injury at the atlanto occipital joint.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses as credible, finding their testimonies consistent and corroborating each other, particularly PW-6's testimony being a clinching piece of evidence.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 15.11.2001; Trial judgment: 24.02.2005; High Court decision: 21.06.2007; Supreme Court decision: 06 February 2024
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Gaurav Agrawal, D. Abhinav Rao, Ms. Prerna Robin, Rahul Jajoo, Devadipta Das, Advs. Counsel for the State: Sirajudeen, Sr. Adv., Krishna Kumar Singh, Sri Harsha Peechara, Duvvuri Subrahmanya Bhanu, Ms. Pallavi, Ms. Kriti Sinha, Akshat Kulshreshtha, Rajiv Kumar Choudhry, G.Seshagiri Rao, Gaichangpou Gangmei, Rahul Aggarwal, Amit Pratap Singh, Ms. Lothungbeni T. Lotha, Yimyanger Longkumer, Advs.
investigation_status: FIR registered (Exhibit P-32), charge sheet filed on 09.01.2002, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Section 302/34; High Court: Initially acquitted, then confirmed conviction; Supreme Court: Upheld conviction of A-1, A-2, and A-4; Modified conviction of A-3 to Section 304 Part II
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused 1 to 4, belonging to the same family, were involved in the murder of the deceased due to political animosity. They alleged that A-1 stopped the auto-rickshaw, dragged the deceased to A-4's house, and all four accused assaulted the deceased with various weapons, leading to his death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that A-3 did not share a common intention to commit murder. They contended that A-3 only used a stone to assault the deceased and did not participate in the initial dragging or weapon-based assault, and that the courts mechanically inferred his involvement under Section 34.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that for an offence under Section 302 IPC, there must be a common intention to cause death. If the accused did not share this intention, they may be convicted under Section 304 Part II IPC instead.
precedent_relied_upon: Camilo Vaz v. State of Goa, [2000] 2 SCR 1088 : (2000) 9 SCC 1; Bawa Singh v. State of Punjab 1993 Supp (2) SCC 754; Sarup Singh v. State of Haryana (2009) 16 SCC 479; Ghana Pradhan & Ors. v. State of Orissa 1991 Supp (2) SCC 451
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the determination that A-3 did not share the common intention to commit murder, but his participation in the assault with a stone made him culpable under Section 304 Part II IPC, leading to a 10-year imprisonment.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, who were part of the same family, were involved in a political dispute with the victim, who was from the same village. On 15.11.2001, the victim was traveling in an auto-rickshaw when the accused stopped the vehicle and dragged the victim to the house of one of the accused. The accused then assaulted the victim with various weapons, including an axe, sword, stone, and knife, leading to the victim's death. The prosecution presented eyewitness accounts, a post-mortem report, and recovered weapons as evidence. The trial court and High Court convicted all four accused of murder under Section 302 IPC, but the Supreme Court modified the conviction of one accused to culpable homicide not amounting to murder under Section 304 Part II IPC due to insufficient evidence of a common intention to commit murder.

title: ATUL THAKUR versus STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH ETC. ETC.
respondent: STATE OF HIMACHAL PRADESH ETC. ETC.
case_title: Atul Thakur v. State of Himachal Pradesh Etc.
mitigating_circumstances: Sudden fight, heat of passion, no premeditation
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304 Part II, sentenced to 5 years imprisonment and fine of Rs.10,000/-
offence_finally_established: Culpable homicide not amounting to murder
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim were friends who had gathered at a house for a drink party. A sudden fight erupted between them after the victim blew smoke on the accused's face. In the heat of passion, the accused attacked the victim with a knife, inflicting six injuries. The accused then offered the victim water and took him to the hospital, where the victim later succumbed to his injuries. The accused informed the victim's father about the incident and stayed at the hospital until the victim's last rites were performed. The prosecution argued that the accused's actions resulted in the victim's death, while the defense claimed the incident was a sudden fight without premeditation.
offence_severity: 5 years rigorous imprisonment to 10 years rigorous imprisonment with fine
physical_harm: Six knife blows causing serious injuries leading to death
number_of_offences: Two counts charged, one upheld
premeditation_planning: No premeditation, act done in heat of passion
motive: Trivial motive of smoke blown on face
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence clearly establishes that the appellant assaulted the deceased without any premeditation. The whole incident took place suddenly and, in the heat of passion, a sudden quarrel started as the deceased, while smoking, blew smoke on the face of the appellant. Resultantly, the appellant got enraged. He told him that he was senior in age and thus should not smoke in his presence much less blow the smoke towards him. Then a sudden physical fight started between them, in which the appellant, in heat of passion, gave six knife blows to the deceased on different parts of his body.
witness_credibility: The evidence of PW-11 and PW-12 (eye-witnesses) would establish that the appellant and others including deceased Hitesh Thakur had gathered at the spot for a drink party arranged at the instance of Hitesh Thakur. They had consumed drinks when the incident took place. Soon after assaulting Hitesh Thakur by knife, when the appellant realised that Hitesh has been badly injured, he offered him water and took him to the hospital along with his other friends. He was in the hospital till Hitesh Thakur succumbed to the injuries. He had also informed the father of Hitesh on telephone and called him to the hospital.
post_offence_conduct: After realising his mistake, he immediately offered water to Hitesh Thakur and also took him to hospital and stayed there till his last rites were performed. PW-2 father of deceased Hitesh Thakur also corroborates the position that the appellant had contacted him to inform that Hitesh had been brought to the hospital in serious condition.
trial_duration: Offence: 27.07.2011; Trial judgment: 31.12.2014; High Court decision: 01.04.2016; Supreme Court decision: 19.01.2018
legal_representation: Aditya Dhawan, Ms. Kiran Dhawan, Chander Shekhar Ashri, Advs. for the Appellant; D. K. Thakur, AAG, Shariq Ahmed, Ms. Taiba Khan, Ajay Marwah, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under s.304 Part II; High Court: Convicted under s.302; Supreme Court: Partly allowed appeals, restored Trial Court's conviction under s.304 Part II with enhanced sentence
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant caused six injuries to the deceased by attacking him with a knife on the fateful night in the presence of their friends who had gathered at the house of accused no.2 for celebrating a drink party arranged at the behest of the deceased. The deceased succumbed to the injuries caused by the appellant.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the appellant acted in the heat of passion without premeditation and did not intend to cause the death of the deceased. The appellant offered water to the deceased, took him to the hospital, and stayed until the deceased's last rites were performed, indicating no intention to cause death.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that culpable homicide not amounting to murder is applicable when the act is committed in the heat of passion without premeditation and without taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel manner.
precedent_relied_upon: Surain Singh v. State of Punjab (2017) 5 SCC 796
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the nature of the offence and the trivial reason for the appellant's rage and assault, along with the use of a knife and multiple blows, did not warrant a light punishment. The sentence period should not be less than 10 years imprisonment with fine to meet the ends of justice.
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court weighed the appellant's actions in the heat of passion, the lack of premeditation, and the fact that the appellant offered water to the deceased and took him to the hospital.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for 10 years with a fine of Rs.10,000/-, in default to undergo further imprisonment for one year. The appellant is entitled to set off under Section 428 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused and the victim were friends who had gathered at a house for a drink party. A sudden fight erupted between them after the victim blew smoke on the accused's face. In the heat of passion, the accused attacked the victim with a knife, inflicting six injuries. The accused then offered the victim water and took him to the hospital, where the victim later succumbed to his injuries. The accused informed the victim's father about the incident and stayed at the hospital until the victim's last rites were performed. The prosecution argued that the accused's actions resulted in the victim's death, while the defense claimed the incident was a sudden fight without premeditation.

title: STATE THROUGH DEPUTY SUPERINTENDENT OF POLICE versus R. SOUNDIRARASU ETC.
petitioner: STATE THROUGH DEPUTY SUPERINTENDENT OF POLICE
case_title: State Through Deputy Superintendent Of Police v. R. Soundirarasu Etc.
statutory_provisions: PC Act s.13(2) r/w 13(1)(e); IPC s.109
offence_finally_established: Criminal misconduct under PC Act s.13(2) r/w 13(1)(e)
neutral_facts: The accused, a public servant, was investigated for acquiring assets disproportionate to his known sources of income. A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against him for alleged criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. During the investigation, the role of his wife as an abettor surfaced. A charge sheet was filed, and the accused filed a petition under Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeking discharge. The Special Judge rejected the petition, finding a prima facie case against the accused.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 months to maximum 3 years imprisonment
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Two offences/counts charged and two were finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the FIR and the evidence of disproportionate assets held by the accused, including the construction of a house, purchase of a building, and transfer of property to the accused's minor son, which were deemed disproportionate to their known sources of income.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the investigating officer, as credible and noted that the explanation offered by the accused was not sufficient to dismiss the charge, as the burden of proof lay on the accused to account for the assets.
trial_duration: FIR registered on 19.09.2005; charge sheet filed; Special Judge rejected petition under s.239; High Court discharged respondents; Supreme Court allowed appeals, directed Special Court to frame charges and put accused to trial
legal_representation: V. Krishnamurthy, AAG, Dr. Joseph Aristotle S., Nupur Sharma, Shobhit Dwivedi, Sanjeev Kumar Mahara, Ms. Richa Vishwakarma, Advs. for the Appellant; K. investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; investigation completed; charge framed
appeal_history: Trial court: Discharged accused under s.239; High Court: Discharged accused; Supreme Court: Allowed appeals, set aside High Court orders, directed trial

defence_argument: The defence argued that the High Court had incorrectly discharged the accused, as the charge against them was not groundless. They claimed that the accused had provided satisfactory explanations for their assets and that the High Court had improperly considered the explanation offered by the accused.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the burden of proof lies on the prosecution to establish that the accused was in possession of properties disproportionate to his known sources of income, which are sources known to the prosecution. The Court also emphasized that the stage of Section 239 of the CrPC requires a prima facie case to be considered, not a full evaluation of the evidence.

neutral_facts_raw: The accused, a public servant, was investigated for acquiring assets disproportionate to his known sources of income. A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against him for alleged criminal misconduct under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988. During the investigation, the role of his wife as an abettor surfaced. A charge sheet was filed, and the accused filed a petition under Section 239 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, seeking discharge. The Special Judge rejected the petition, finding a prima facie case against the accused. The High Court discharged the accused, but the Supreme Court overturned this decision, stating that the charge was not groundless and that the accused should be put to trial.

title: IMRAT SINGH & ORS. versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH
case_title: Imrat Singh & Ors. v. State of Madhya Pradesh
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of murder and culpable homicide
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleges that on May 25, 1994, at approximately 2 pm, the accused were seen beating the victim with lathis. Two eyewitnesses, who were returning from a village, reported the incident and fled due to threats from the accused. They later filed an FIR at the police station. The investigation was deemed unfair, and the witnesses had criminal antecedents. The court also noted that the witnesses had changed their statements over time, raising doubts about their reliability. The court concluded that the prosecution's case was not sufficiently supported by the evidence and that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the accused.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment and two years rigorous imprisonment for the offence punishable under Section 148 IPC
physical_harm: The deceased was beaten to death with lathis
number_of_offences: Charged under Sections 148 and 302 r/w 149 IPC; finally upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court did not accept the testimony of the main witnesses PW10 and PW11 due to contradictions and inconsistencies in their statements, and questioned the fairness of the investigation.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PW10 and PW11) as unreliable due to contradictions in their statements, their improving statements over time, and the lack of consistency in their accounts of the incident and attending circumstances.
bail_history: Accused are on bail. Their bail bonds are discharged.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 25.05.1994; Trial judgment: 30.03.1995; High Court decision: 24.10.2008; Supreme Court decision: 24.10.2019
legal_representation: Shikhil Suri, Adv. (A.C.), Ms. June Chaudhary, Sr. Adv., Mohd. Parvez Dabas, Uzmi Jameel Husain, Ms. Shilpa Saini, Shakil Ahmed Syed, Advs. for the Appellants; Rahul Kaushik, Ms. Bhuvneshwari Pathak, Ms. Shilpi Satyapriya Satyam, Advs. for the Respondent
investigation_status: FIR recorded after visiting the spot by the police; site plan prepared; investigation not fair
procedural_irregularity: The manner in which the site plan was prepared clearly indicates that the investigation was not a fair investigation
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeal allowed, conviction set aside, accused acquitted
prosecution_argument: The prosecution relied mainly on the testimony of two eye-witnesses, PW10 and PW11, who claimed to have seen the accused beating Gajraj Singh with lathis. The FIR was recorded after the police visited the spot, and the witnesses were treated as credible eye-witnesses.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the testimonies of PW10 and PW11 are untrustworthy and contradictory. They also pointed out that the investigation was not fair, and many important witnesses were not examined. The witnesses had criminal antecedents, and there was enmity between the parties, which could have led to false accusations.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the prosecution must establish the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt, and that contradictions in witness statements and flaws in the investigation can cast doubt on the reliability of the conviction.
precedent_relied_upon: Not stated
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
judicial_mitigating_factors: The court considered the contradictions in the witness statements, the possibility of a concocted prosecution story, the presence of enmity, and the criminal antecedents of the witnesses.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution alleges that on May 25, 1994, at approximately 2 pm, the accused were seen beating the victim with lathis. Two eyewitnesses, who were returning from a village, reported the incident and fled due to threats from the accused. They later filed an FIR at the police station. The trial court and high court relied heavily on the testimonies of these two witnesses, which were considered credible. However, the Supreme Court found contradictions in the testimonies of these witnesses, as well as inconsistencies in the FIR and site plan. The investigation was deemed unfair, and the witnesses had criminal antecedents. The court also noted that the witnesses had changed their statements over time, raising doubts about their reliability. The court concluded that the prosecution's case was not sufficiently supported by the evidence and that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the accused.

title: NITYA NAND  versus STATE OF U.P. & ANR.
case_title: Nitya Nand v. State of U.P. & Anr.
neutral_facts: The accused, along with others, were part of an unlawful assembly with the common object of eliminating the deceased by criminal force. The deceased was assaulted by the other accused persons with weapons such as kanta and knives, resulting in his death. The accused in question fired a shot from a country-made pistol into the air to frighten the witnesses and then fled the scene. The post-mortem report confirmed multiple injuries on the deceased, indicating the assault was homicidal. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the involvement of the accused in the unlawful assembly and the murder.
offence_severity: Imprisonment for life under Section 302/149 IPC
physical_harm: Multiple injuries leading to death
number_of_offences: Charges under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC were finally upheld
motive: Old enmity due to property dispute
key_evidence_accepted: Appellant was roped in by virtue of ss.148 and 149 IPC as a member of the unlawful assembly which had the common object of eliminating the deceased by criminal force.
witness_credibility: PW-1 and PW-2 (sons of the deceased) were eyewitnesses whose testimony was considered credible and unflinching, despite cross-examination.
bail_history: This Court granted leave but rejected the prayer for bail.
trial_duration: Offence: 08.09.1992; Trial judgment: 20.01.1997; High Court decision: 27.09.2012; Supreme Court decision: 04 September 2024
legal_representation: P. K. Jain, Saurabh Jain, S.P. Singh Rathore, P.K. Goswami, Jagannath Jha, Arunansh Bharti Goswami, Advs. for the Appellant; Goutham Shivhankar, Ms. Ruchira Goel, Adit Jayeshbhai Shah, Sharanya Sinha, Ms. Manju Jetley, Advs. for the Respondents
investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the appellant was part of an unlawful assembly and that the eyewitnesses PW-1 and PW-2 stated that the appellant was carrying a country-made pistol and fired in the air to frighten the informant and others, thereby enabling the accused to escape. The prosecution also emphasized the motive rooted in property disputes and old enmity between the families.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution failed to prove the appellant's involvement in the actual murder, as there were no firearm injuries, no recovery of a country-made pistol or cartridges, and the scribe Kuldeep Kumar Tiwari and Laxmi Narain, who could have provided crucial evidence, were not examined as witnesses. The defence also claimed the conviction was based on mere suspicion.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle under Section 149 IPC, which holds that every member of an unlawful assembly is vicariously liable for the offence committed in prosecution of the common object, even if they did not directly participate in the act.
precedent_relied_upon: Krishnappa v. State of Karnataka [2012] 6 SCR 1068 : (2012) 11 SCC 237; Vinubhai Ranchhodbhai Patel v. Rajivbhai Dudabhai Patel [2018] 6 SCR 1050 : (2018) 7 SCC 743; Yunis alias Kariya Vs. State of M.P. (2003) 1 SCC 425
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution proved the charges against the appellant under Sections 148 and 302/149 IPC beyond reasonable doubt, and the appellant was deemed a member of the unlawful assembly with a common object of eliminating the deceased.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, along with others, were part of an unlawful assembly with the common object of eliminating the deceased by criminal force. The deceased was assaulted by the other accused persons with weapons such as kanta and knives, resulting in his death. The accused in question fired a shot from a country-made pistol into the air to frighten the witnesses and then fled the scene. The post-mortem report confirmed multiple injuries on the deceased, indicating the assault was homicidal. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts and medical evidence to establish the involvement of the accused in the unlawful assembly and the murder.

title: RAM CHANDRA BHAGAT versus STATE OF JHARKHAND
case_title: RAM CHANDRA BHAGAT v. STATE OF JHARKHAND
neutral_facts: The accused and the victim lived together for nine years and had two children. The accused had executed an agreement with the victim stating his intention to marry her and had filed an application for marriage registration under the Special Marriage Act. Official documents, including voter lists, showed the victim as the accused's wife. Despite not performing a formal marriage ritual, the accused and the victim cohabited and had a child, leading to the prosecution's claim that the accused had deceived the victim into believing they were married. The accused denied the agreement and claimed the victim was not his wife.
offence_severity: imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine
physical_harm: Not stated
number_of_offences: Charged under Section 493 IPC; upheld by trial court, appellate court, and High Court

The accused had executed an agreement of marriage and filed an application for registration of their marriage under the Special Marriage Act. In several official documents, she had been shown to be the wife of the accused.
witness_credibility: The witnesses appeared in the Court and supported the relationship of the accused with the complainant as husband and wife. The accused accepted her as his wife in writing in presence of the witnesses.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: not stated; Trial judgment: not stated; High Court decision: 08.09.2005; Supreme Court decision: 24.11.2010
legal_representation: Deba Prasad Mukherjee for the Appellant; D Ratan Kumar Chaudhary for the Respondent
investigation_status: Charge sheet filed; Trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction; High Court: Upheld conviction; Supreme Court: Appeal placed before Chief Justice of India for referral to another Bench
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused had deceitfully induced the complainant to believe that they were lawfully married, leading to cohabitation and the birth of two children, thereby fulfilling the ingredients of Section 493 of the Indian Penal Code.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the accused did not deceive the complainant into believing they were lawfully married, as there was no formal marriage ceremony or registration, and the complainant was not under the belief of a lawful marriage.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that a criminal statute must be construed strictly, and all ingredients of the section must be satisfied for an offence to be established.
precedent_relied_upon: Moideenkutty Haji and others Vs. Kunhikoya and others, AIR 1987 Kerala 184; Dr. A.N. Mukerji Vs. State, AIR 1969 Allahabad 489

title: JAGJIT SINGH versus STATE OF PUNJAB
case_title: JAGJIT SINGH v. STATE OF PUNJAB
statutory_provisions: IPC s.304-B, s.113-B of Evidence Act
aggravating_circumstances: Cruelty and harassment for dowry demand
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.304-B IPC, sentence reduced to 7 years
high_court_outcome: Affirmed conviction, reduced sentence to 7 years
neutral_facts: The accused, a man, was married to a woman who died along with her child by drowning in a river within seven years of their marriage. The prosecution alleged that the accused subjected the deceased to cruelty and harassment related to dowry demands. The deceased visited her sister's house and called her father, reporting harassment. The father and sister testified about the harassment, and a doctor opined that the death occurred around February 16-17, 2001. The accused claimed there was no cruelty or dowry demand, but the courts found the evidence of harassment sufficient to invoke the presumption under s.113-B of the Evidence Act.
offence_severity: Minimum 6 years, Maximum 7 years rigorous imprisonment
physical_harm: The deceased and her child died by drowning
number_of_offences: Charged under Section 304-B IPC; upheld by High Court
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the testimony of PW-1 and PW-3 regarding dowry harassment, and the evidence of PW-5 that he saw the deceased weeping at the PCO on 16.02.2001. The Court also considered the post-mortem report indicating the probable time of death.
witness_credibility: The Court stated that the credibility of witnesses as assessed by the lower courts is not ordinarily reappraised by this Court, and the findings of the trial court and High Court were accepted as final unless vitiated by errors of law or procedure.

Further investigation revealed that the said IMEI was used for the mobile phone SIM 9818480558 belonging to the accused-appellant immediately after the murder of the victim-deceased. This helped the police in apprehending the appellant and in recovery of three mobile handsets, one of which bore the IMEI no.35136304044030. neutral_facts: The accused, who was married and had one son aged about 20 years and two daughters aged 22 years and 13 years respectively, killed his wife and three children by pouring petrol on their persons and setting them on fire. The incident occurred 25-27 years after the marriage. The accused was last seen with his wife at about midnight and was in fact quarreling with her at that time. The incident happened at 4 or 4.30 a.m., with a time gap of about 4 hours between the last seen time and the incident. The accused was found with cash of Rs.7,68,080/- and several items of clothing, but his alibi was deemed false. A 10-litre white plastic can with petrol was found at the scene, indicating the accused had brought petrol to the scene. The accused was found with a red bucket used for pouring petrol on the victims, which was confirmed by a chemical analysis. The prosecution's case relied on circumstantial evidence, including the presence of the accused at the scene, the petrol can, and the absence of any other plausible explanation for the crime.

The accused had pre-planned the diabolical and gruesome murder in a dastardly manner. He did not act on any spur of the moment. He cannot be reformed and rehabilitated. Thus, the penalty of death sentence is upheld.
defence_argument: The accused submitted that he left the scene as he had received a message that his sister in Delhi who was suffering from cancer had become critical, and thus, he rushed from Mumbai to be with her. The accused also claimed that the recovery of the red bucket was a fabrication by the police and that the prosecution failed to prove motive.
legal_principle_applied: Death sentence should only be given in the rarest of rare cases. The Court has to further enquire and believe that the accused cannot be reformed or rehabilitated and shall continue with his criminal acts. A balance sheet is to be prepared in considering the imposition of death penalty of the aggravating and mitigating circumstances, and a just balance is to be struck.

sentencing_rationale: The accused burnt living persons to death which is a horrible act causing excruciating pain to the victim, and this could not have been unknown to the accused. The accused did not act on any spur of the moment provocation. There was a quarrel between accused and his wife at midnight, but the accused having brought a large quantity of petrol into his residential apartment shows that he had pre-planned the diabolical and gruesome murder in a dastardly manner. Such person who instead of protecting his family kills them in such a cruel and barbaric manner cannot be reformed or rehabilitated. Balance sheet is heavily against him. They also claimed that the prosecution did not establish that the death was not accidental and that the accused did not meet the reverse onus of proof.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the initial burden of proving a dowry death lies with the prosecution, and if that burden is met, the accused must rebut the presumption by proving the death was accidental.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found that the ingredients of Section 304-B of the IPC were met, and the accused failed to rebut the presumption of dowry death. title: ALAMELU & ANR. versus STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
respondent: STATE REPRESENTED BY INSPECTOR OF POLICE
case_title: Alamelu & Anr. v. State Represented by Inspector of Police
statutory_provisions: IPC s.366, s.376 read with s.109
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that PW-2, the daughter of PW-1, was abducted and subjected to forcible marriage and rape by A-1 and others. The accused were charged under Sections 366 and 376 of the IPC. The victim's account of the abduction and marriage was questioned, with the court noting that she did not protest or seek help despite having opportunities to do so. The court also highlighted the lack of reliable evidence to confirm the victim's age and the absence of corroboration for her testimony.
offence_severity: 3 years to life imprisonment
physical_harm: Rape and sexual intercourse
number_of_offences: 8 counts charged, 8 counts upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The entire story about the abduction by car and the forced marriage was seemingly concocted. Even after the alleged marriage with A-1, PW-2 continued to be a willing partner in the entire episode. She did not protest nor made any complaint though she had the opportunity to do so on many occasions. The conduct of PW-2 from the time of her alleged abduction till the time of her alleged recovery was not natural for a girl who had been compelled to marry and subjected to illicit sexual intercourse.
witness_credibility: The testimony of PW-2 does not satisfy the test of being free from basic infirmities or improbabilities. The conduct of PW-2 and the inconsistencies in her testimony, along with the father's lack of involvement and the absence of reliable evidence regarding the transfer certificate, cast doubt on the credibility of the main witnesses.
post_offence_conduct: PW-2 did not make any complaint on so many occasions when she had the opportunity to do so. She did not raise any protest or complain to anyone at any of the stages after being allegedly abducted. She did not make any complaint at the residence of Selvi, sister of A-1, or when she was taken to the house of PW5 or to the police station.
trial_duration: Charge-sheet filed against A-1 for offences punishable under Sections 366 and 376 IPC and accused Nos. 2 to 8 for offences punishable under Sections 366 and 376 read with Section 109 IPC. The trial court convicted all the accused. The conviction was affirmed by the High Court.
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused and the State in the Supreme Court not specified
investigation_status: Charge-sheet filed against A-1 for offences punishable under Sections 366 and 376 IPC and accused Nos. 2 to 8 for offences punishable under Sections 366 and 376 read with Section 109 IPC
procedural_irregularity: The trial court as well as the High Court failed to take into consideration the inherent improbabilities in the case sought to be projected by the prosecution. The findings recorded by both the Courts below were perverse and unsupportable by the evidence on record.
appeal_history: The conviction of the accused-appellants was challenged on the ground that the conclusions reached by both the Courts below were perverse and that they ignored the inconsistencies and contradictions in the evidence of the witnesses. It was contended that the facts of the case clearly suggested that there was no question of any abduction, forcible marriage or rape. Per contra, the State contended that the prosecution version was consistent and further that, in exercise of its powers under Article 136 of the Constitution, the Supreme Court normally does not interfere with the concurrent findings recorded by the Courts below and, thus, the instant appeals were liable to be dismissed. Allowance of the appeals, the Court held: Even though the powers of this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution are very wide, but in criminal appeals, this Court would not interfere with the concurrent findings of facts, save in very exceptional cases.
prosecution_argument: The prosecution alleged that PW-2 was abducted, forcibly married, and raped by A-1, with PW-2 being a minor at the relevant date. The prosecution version was consistent and sought to implicate the accused in the alleged abduction, forced marriage, and rape.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the entire story of abduction and forced marriage was concocted. PW-2's father suspected she was romantically involved with A-1, and her disappearance was presumed to be his responsibility. The conduct of PW-2 was unnatural for a girl who had been compelled to marry and subjected to illicit sexual intercourse.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the assessment of evidence by the High Court is accepted as final unless the conclusions are manifestly perverse and unsupportable by the evidence on record. It also emphasized that corroboration is not a sine qua non for conviction in rape cases if the victim's testimony does not suffer from basic infirmities or improbabilities.
precedent_relied_upon: Birad Mal Singhvi v. Anand Purohit, 1988 (Suppl.) SCC 604; Narbada Devi Gupta v. Birendra Kumar Jaiswal, (2003) 8 SCC 745; Jaya Mala v. Home Secretary, Government of Jammu & Kashmir & Ors., (1982) 2 SCC 538; Ravinder Singh Gorkhi v. State of U.P., (2006) 5 SCC 584; Rameshwar v. State of Rajasthan, (1952) SCR 377
sentencing_rationale: Not applicable
judicial_mitigating_factors: The conduct of PW-2, including her willingness to stay with A-1 after the alleged marriage and not making any complaints despite having opportunities to do so, was considered.
other_sentence_order: The accused-appellants were acquitted and directed to be released forthwith.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution alleged that PW-2, the daughter of PW-1, was abducted and subjected to forcible marriage and rape by A-1 and others. The accused were charged under Sections 366 and 376 of the IPC. The trial court convicted all accused, and the High Court affirmed the conviction. However, the Supreme Court found the prosecution's version of events to be inconsistent and improbable. The victim's account of the abduction and marriage was questioned, with the court noting that she did not protest or seek help despite having opportunities to do so. The court also highlighted the lack of reliable evidence to confirm the victim's age and the absence of corroboration for her testimony. The court ultimately acquitted the accused, finding the prosecution's case to be fabricated.

The body was later recovered from the field, and the victim was found to have sustained fatal injuries. legal_principle_applied: The principle of 'cognate offences' was applied, which holds that where an accused is charged with a grave offence, he can be punished for a less grave offence if the grave offence is not proved, provided the ingredients of the lesser offence are independently satisfied.

title: ARUMUGAM versus THE STATE REPRESENTED BY ITS INSPECTOR OF  POLICE
respondent: THE STATE REPRESENTED BY ITS INSPECTOR OF  POLICE
case_title: Arumugam v. State of Madras
aggravating_circumstances: Accused was annoyed with the victim, motive of low character
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment
neutral_facts: The accused, who was an agriculturist, murdered his step mother during agricultural operations in a field. The accused told his step sister that he had strangled and killed the victim. He later made an extra-judicial confession to a Village Administrative Officer, which was recorded in writing. A rope used for strangulation was recovered. The victim's body was found in a decomposed state, and the post-mortem examination indicated that the cause of death was asphyxia due to strangulation. The medical evidence supported the ocular evidence, and the accused had prepared for the act by hiding the rope in the field.
offence_severity: Life imprisonment
physical_harm: Death caused by strangulation
number_of_offences: One offence charged and upheld
premeditation_planning: The court found the accused was annoyed with the deceased and had premeditated the act
motive: The accused suspected the deceased of being of low character and an embarrassment to him
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court accepted the extra-judicial confession of the accused, the medical evidence supporting the cause of death as asphyxia due to strangulation, and the recovery of the rope used for strangulation.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses, including the step sister (PW5) and the Village Administrative Officer (PW1), as credible, noting that PW5's statement supported the motive and the accused's annoyance with the deceased, while PW1's recording of the confession was reliable.
post_offence_conduct: The accused did not try to run away after making the extra-judicial confession and was handed over to the police by PW1 at about 6 p.m.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 19th March 2000; Trial judgment: 01.09.2005; High Court decision: 2001; Supreme Court decision: 2010
legal_representation: Venkat Subramanyam, V. K. Sidharthan, Anup Kumar for the Appellant; S. Thananjayan for the Respondent

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution's case was supported by the extra-judicial confession, the recovery of the rope, and the medical evidence, which confirmed the cause of death as strangulation.

title: SUBODH NATH AND ANR. versus STATE OF TRIPURA
case_title: Subodh Nath and Anr. v. State of Tripura
neutral_facts: The accused, Subodh Nath and Paritosh, were prosecuted for the killing of Ashutosh. The prosecution case was supported by the testimony of an eyewitness, PW-13, who stated that the accused assaulted the deceased with an axe and a lathi, and that the accused later shot the deceased with a gun. PW-13 fled the scene due to fear of the accused. The evidence of PW-13 was corroborated by PW-6, who found the deceased and the accused grazing cows in the jungle. The Investigating Officer recovered an axe handle near the deceased's body.
offence_severity: Death caused by an axe and a gun, punishable under Section 302 IPC
physical_harm: Injuries on the dead body caused by an axe and a gun
number_of_offences: One offence charged, one upheld
key_evidence_accepted: The evidence of PW-13 is corroborated by the evidence of PW-6, the Investigating Officer (PW-19), and the inquest report (Ext. P-2), which show injuries on the deceased caused by an axe and a gun, and the recovery of the axe handle.
witness_credibility: The court found PW-13's evidence reliable despite discrepancies, noting that normal discrepancies in witness accounts are expected and do not automatically cast doubt on credibility unless they are material.
post_offence_conduct: PW-13 ran away from the place of occurrence due to fear of the appellants who had threatened him, but this was explained as a result of his fear and not as an indication of unreliability.
trial_duration: Offence: 09.10.1998; Trial judgment: 08.06.2005; High Court decision: 08.06.2005; Supreme Court decision: 19.03.2013

appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction upheld; High Court: Conviction upheld; Supreme Court: Appeal of appellant No.2 allowed, appeal of appellant No.1 dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused were guilty of the offence under Section 302/34 IPC, supported by the testimony of an eye-witness, PW-13, and corroborated by other evidence such as the recovery of the weapon and the inquest report. They also contended that the motive to kill was not established, but argued that direct evidence of the offence was sufficient.
defence_argument: The defence argued that appellant No.2 was below 18 years of age at the time of the offence and thus a juvenile under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, and that the 2000 Act should apply. They also claimed that the conviction of appellant No.1 was based on an unreliable sole witness, PW-13, who had run away from the scene and was a suspect, and that there were discrepancies in the evidence, lack of weapon recovery, and no established motive.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000, applies to offences committed prior to its commencement if the accused was below 18 years of age at the time of the offence. It also emphasized that discrepancies in witness accounts are not sufficient to discard evidence unless they are 'material discrepancies' creating reasonable doubt.

sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed based on the conviction that the accused were guilty of the offence under Section 302/34 IPC, with the court upholding the trial court's and High Court's conviction and sentence for appellant No.1, while remitting the case of appellant No.2 to the Juvenile Justice Board.
other_sentence_order: The case of appellant No.2 was remitted to the Juvenile Justice Board of North Tripura district for disposal in accordance with the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000.

PW-13 fled the scene due to fear of the accused. The evidence of PW-13 was corroborated by PW-6, who found the deceased and the accused grazing cows in the jungle. The Investigating Officer recovered an axe handle near the deceased's body. The trial court convicted both accused under s.302/34 IPC, and the High Court upheld the conviction. However, the Supreme Court remitted the case of Paritosh to the Juvenile Justice Board as he was under 18 at the time of the offence, and acquitted Subodh Nath based on the corroborated evidence.

title: NARESH KUMAR versus STATE OF HARYANA & ORS.

The accused's conduct, including his false name during arrest and absence of a valid explanation for his actions, supported the prosecution's case. title: DHAN SINGH versus STATE OF HARYANA
case_title: Ohan Singh v. State of Haryana
neutral_facts: The prosecution case was that the deceased had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. On the date of the incident, the deceased, his wife, and his daughters were present in the house. The brother of the deceased gave a lathi blow on other parts of the body of the deceased. Other accused also inflicted lathi blows on the deceased's back. Injuries were also inflicted on the deceased's wife. The accused persons then ran away. The injured were taken to the hospital. The Head Constable recorded the statement of the deceased, which was later treated as a dying declaration. The deceased died in the hospital after a few days. The case was converted into one under Section 302 IPC.
offence_severity: Minimum 10 years rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 20,000/-
physical_harm: Deceased suffered head injury with iron rod, lathi blows on other parts of body, injuries on wife and daughter
number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged, conviction under s. 304 (Part II) upheld
premeditation_planning: Court found no premeditation or planning
key_evidence_accepted: The dying declaration of the deceased, which was clear and satisfactory, was fully corroborated by medical evidence. The statement was recorded by the Head Constable, who was competent to do so at the relevant time, and the deceased was declared fit to make the statement by the doctor.
witness_credibility: The wife and daughter of the deceased were declared hostile, but this by itself would not demolish the prosecution's case. The Court emphasized that the prosecution had sufficient evidence to establish the guilt of the accused beyond any reasonable doubt.
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 15.07.1997; Trial judgment: 17.05.1999; High Court decision: 30.04.2008; Supreme Court decision: 22.07.2010
legal_representation: Counsel for the accused: Biswajit Swain (for Rajesh Prasad Singh); Counsel for the State: B.S. Mor (for T.V. George)
investigation_status: FIR registered under Sections 148, 452, 323, 506 read with Section 149 IPC; case converted into one under Section 302 IPC; charge sheet filed under sections 148, 149, 323, 506, 452 and 302 IPC; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Convicted under Sections 148, 149, 323, 506, 452 and 302 IPC; High Court: Refused to interfere with the order of trial court; Supreme Court: Partly allowed the appeal, altered conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 (Part II) IPC
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the deceased had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. The accused, including the brother of the deceased and the appellant, attacked the deceased, with the appellant inflicting a blow on the head with an iron rod. The deceased's statement, recorded by the Head Constable, was treated as a dying declaration and was found to be clear and satisfactory, corroborated by medical evidence. The prosecution maintained that the deceased's statement was reliable and that the appellant's actions led to the deceased's death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the statement recorded by the Head Constable was not reliable as a dying declaration, as it should have been recorded by a Magistrate. They also contended that the son and daughter of the deceased were not examined as witnesses, and the findings were based on no evidence. The defence further argued that the conviction should have been under Section 304 (Part II) IPC and not under Section 302 IPC.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that a dying declaration is admissible under Section 32 of the Evidence Act if it is made by a person as to the cause of his death or such circumstances. The Court also considered the intention of the accused and whether the act was committed with the intention to kill or with knowledge that it was likely to cause death.
precedent_relied_upon: Dalip Singh v. State of Punjab (1979) 4 SCC 332; Cherlopalli Cheliminabi Sahed v. State of A.P. (2003) 2 SCC 571; Kanti Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2004) 10 SCC 113; Jagriti Devi v. State of H.P. (2009) 14 SCC 771; Gurmukh Singh v. State of Haryana (2009) 15 SCC 635
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the Court found that the appellant had no intention to kill the deceased and did not give him a blow with the intention to kill or with knowledge that it was likely to cause death. Therefore, the offence was altered from Section 302 to Section 304 (Part II) IPC.
other_sentence_order: The appellant was awarded rigorous imprisonment for a period of 10 years and a fine of Rs. 20,000/-. In default of payment of fine, the accused shall undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of six months.
neutral_facts_raw: The prosecution case was that the deceased had a dispute with his brother over a residential house. On the date of the incident, the deceased, his wife, and his daughters were present in the house. The accused persons, including the brother of the deceased and the appellant, entered the house. The appellant was holding an iron rod and inflicted a blow on the head of the deceased. The brother of the deceased gave a lathi blow on other parts of the body of the deceased. Other accused also inflicted lathi blows on the deceased's back. Injuries were also inflicted on the deceased's wife. The accused persons then ran away. The injured were taken to the hospital. The Head Constable recorded the statement of the deceased, which was later treated as a dying declaration. The deceased died in the hospital after a few days. The case was converted into one under Section 302 IPC. The trial court found that the head injury attributed to the appellant was sufficient to cause the death of the deceased and convicted the appellant under Sections 148, 149, 323, 506, 452, and 302 IPC. The High Court refused to interfere with the trial court's order.

respondent: THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH (NOW STATE OF CHHATTISGARH)
case_title: KAMAL PRASAD & ORS. v. THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH (NOW STATE OF CHHATTISGARH)
statutory_provisions: IPC s.148, 302 r/w 149, 307 r/w 149; Explosive Substance Act s.4/5
aggravating_circumstances: Use of explosives, multiple injuries, premeditation

The victim sustained multiple injuries from the blast and later died. The witnesses stated that the accused were present at the scene and participated in the attack. The accused attempted to establish an alibi, but their testimonies lacked corroborative evidence.

number_of_offences: Charges levied against the accused and the sentence as awarded by the Courts below not interfered with
premeditation_planning: The court found that the accused had formed an unlawful assembly and had made preparation for the murder
key_evidence_accepted: Death of the deceased 'C' and his son 'K' is undisputed – Deceased 'C' having sustained multiple injuries upon vital parts of the body as a result of the bombs being thrown at him also stands proved – Testimonies of three witnesses is coherent on material facts such as the presence of the accused on the spot of the crime; the death of the deceased; a blast having taken place; and the accused being the assailants.
witness_credibility: All 3 primary witnesses of the prosecution i.e., PW-3, PW-16, and PW-17 have categorically deposed the presence of the appellants at the spot of the crime and such a statement could not be shaken in cross-examination – The creditworthiness of the witnesses is unimpeachable.
bail_history: Bail granted to the appellants stands cancelled, to surrender
trial_duration: Dates of offence: 17.04.1988; Trial judgment: 11.05.1992; High Court decision: 19.10.2010; Supreme Court decision: 10.10.2023

investigation_status: FIR registered; charge sheet filed; trial completed
appeal_history: Trial court: Conviction affirmed; High Court: Conviction affirmed; Supreme Court: Appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution's case rested primarily on the testimonies of three witnesses, PW-3, PW-16, and PW-17, who categorically deposed the presence of the appellants at the crime scene, the death of the deceased, and the occurrence of a blast. The Court found these testimonies to be coherent, reliable, and unimpeachable, with no force in the contention that they were contradictory.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the prosecution's case was undermined by the delay in filing the FIR, the alleged contradictions in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses, the deceased's history of criminal cases, and the appellants' plea of alibi. legal_principle_applied: The Court applied the principle of preponderance of probability and the standard of 'strict scrutiny' for the plea of alibi. It also emphasized that the burden of proof lies with the prosecution to establish the presence of the accused at the crime scene.

sentencing_rationale: The sentence imposed was found to be justified as it was proportionate to the crimes committed, and the Court did not find any reason to interfere with the sentences awarded by the Trial Court and confirmed by the High Court.

The deceased received burn injuries nine months after marriage and made a dying declaration implicating her husband in the incident. The prosecution contended that the husband had doused her in kerosene and set her on fire, leading to her death.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the medical evidence contradicted the prosecution's narrative, as the deceased's burns were not on the back, which would have been expected if she was doused in kerosene from behind. They also claimed the dying declaration was contradictory and unreliable, with the first part being tutored by the husband.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle under Section 304-B of the Indian Penal Code and Section 113-B of the Evidence Act, which presumes that the accused caused the dowry death if the essential ingredients are proved, including the death occurring within seven years of marriage, not under normal circumstances, and due to cruelty or harassment in connection with dowry demands.
precedent_relied_upon: Hira Lal & Ors. Vs. State (Govt. of NCT), Delhi (2003) 8 SCC 80
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the prosecution successfully proved the dowry death, and the trial court and High Court correctly convicted the accused under Section 304-B IPC. The court also found the accused guilty under Section 498-A IPC for subjecting the deceased to harassment.
neutral_facts_raw: The accused, the husband of the victim, subjected the victim to cruelty and harassment in connection with a demand for dowry. Nine months after their marriage, the victim sustained burn injuries. The next day, she made a dying declaration before a magistrate, initially stating it was an accident, but later alleging that her husband had doused her in kerosene and set her on fire. The victim died 12 days after the incident. The prosecution presented evidence including the victim's dying declaration, the testimony of the victim's parents, and a medical report indicating the cause of death was burns. The trial court convicted the accused under Sections 304-B and 498-A of the IPC, and the High Court upheld the conviction. The Supreme Court affirmed the conviction, finding that the evidence supported the prosecution's case of dowry death and harassment.

title: KRISHAN KUMAR MALIK versus STATE OF HARYANA

title: HARESH MOHANDAS RAJPUT versus STATE OF MAHARASHTRA

witness_credibility: The court assessed the credibility of the witnesses, particularly the child witness Nitesh (PW.3), and found that the circumstances were consistent with the guilt of the accused, with no reasonable ground for concluding innocence.

title: MANOJ AND ANR. versus STATE OF KARNATAKA
case_title: Manoj And Anr. v. State Of Karnataka
trial_court_outcome: Convicted under s.302 and s.506 r/w s.34
high_court_outcome: Confirmed conviction under s.302 r/w s.34, acquitted under s.506 r/w s.34

The deceased succumbed to his injuries after being taken to the hospital. The prosecution relied on eyewitness accounts, medical evidence, and recovered weapons to establish the sequence of events leading to the deceased's death. title: HARILAL ETC. versus STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH (NOW CHHATTISGARH)
case_title: Harilal Etc. v. State of Madhya Pradesh (Now Chhattisgarh)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for life
neutral_facts: The prosecution alleged that three individuals assaulted and killed a man during a night incident. A first information report (FIR) was lodged the next day by a village chowkidar, who was not an eyewitness. Two eyewitnesses testified about the incident, but their accounts were inconsistent with previous statements and lacked details about the severity of the assault. The body was found near a temple, 300 feet away from where the assault allegedly occurred. Medical evidence indicated severe injuries, including head trauma and rib fractures, suggesting a violent attack. The prosecution relied on the discovery of a lathi and blood-stained clothes at the accused's residences, but the evidence was inconclusive regarding the cause of death and the exact manner in which the assault occurred.

physical_harm: The deceased suffered severe injuries including lacerated wounds, contusions, fractures, and internal injuries leading to death due to shock.
number_of_offences: Three offences were charged, but the High Court upheld the conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC.
key_evidence_accepted: The Supreme Court did not accept the testimony of the prosecution witnesses as sufficient to convict the accused for murder, noting inconsistencies and gaps in their accounts, and found the evidence inconclusive regarding the cause of death and the manner in which the murder took place.
witness_credibility: The court assessed the main witnesses (PW-2 and PW-6) as inconsistent and unreliable, noting that their testimonies did not corroborate each other and left significant gaps in the prosecution's story.
